newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Rodriguez says Argentina punished due to defaults.
newsitem.headline: Rodriguez says Argentina punished due to defaults.

text.p: The Argentine Economy Ministry's chief advisor Carlos Rodriguez said Tuesday the country will only improve its country risk ratings when it convinces foreign investors to forget its debt defaults of the 1980s.

Rodriguez told a banking conference in Buenos Aires that Argentina fares worse than neighboring Chile in credit ratings because "countries that did not service their debt regularly in the 1980s are punished."
"What do we have to do to improve this? We have to make them forget," he said.
Rodriguez quoted from a paper written by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that attempted to explain how credit raters like Moody's and Standard & Poor's reached their conclusions.
The paper puts the ratings on a scale of one to 16, with 16 points being the top rating equivalent to S&P's AAA. Seven points and above is investment-grade and below that is speculative grade.
"Our poor country has three from Moody's and five from S&P. In no way do we manage to leave the speculative grade," Rodriguez said in his speech.
"Somebody has to explain to us why we have five and Chile 10," he added.

Rodriguez said the New York Fed paper concluded that indicators such as the fiscal deficit, where Argentina performs well, carried little weight, whereas the debt to exports ratio is given preeminence.
Rodriguez said Argentina's exports were growing quickly as a proportion of debt but the country was still paying for "decades and decades of having a closed economy."
"Our exports and imports are a small part of GDP. With this we easily explain the difference in ratings," the official said.
